title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
summary: Return whether the array can be split into two subsets with equal sums.
statement:
Return `true` if the values of `nums` can be divided into two groups whose sums are equal. Every value must go into exactly one of the groups.

This is the same as asking whether some subset of `nums` sums to exactly half of the total. An odd total can never be split evenly.
hints: If the total is odd, it is impossible. Otherwise you need a subset that adds up to exactly total / 2.
This is 0/1 knapsack: can[s] says whether some subset of the values seen so far sums to s.
For each value v, update can[s] |= can[s − v] for s from target down to v. Going downward ensures each value is used at most once.
explain: The total is 22, so each group must sum to 11. `[1,5,5]` and `[11]` both sum to 11, so the answer is `true`.

title: Target Sum
summary: Put + or − in front of every number. Return how many sign choices make the expression equal target.
statement:
Put either `+` or `-` in front of every number in `nums` and evaluate the resulting expression. Return the number of different sign choices that make the expression equal `target`.

Every number gets exactly one sign. Two assignments are different if any position's sign differs, even when the numbers are equal.
hints: Trying all 2ⁿ sign choices works for n ≤ 20, but there is a neat counting reformulation.
If P is the sum of the numbers marked +, then P − (total − P) = target, so P = (total + target) / 2.

Count the subsets that sum to P with a knapsack count: ways[s] += ways[s − v], iterating s downward. If (total + target) is odd or negative, the answer is 0. Zeros double the count, which the DP handles naturally.
explain: To reach 3 from five 1s, exactly one of them must be negative, for example `-1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 3`. The minus sign can go on any of the 5 numbers, so there are 5 ways.

title: Last Stone Weight II
summary: Smashing stones x ≤ y leaves y − x (or nothing). Choose the pairs freely. Return the smallest possible weight of the last stone (0 if none remain).
statement:
Each value in `stones` is the weight of a stone. You repeatedly choose any two stones, with weights `x ≤ y`, and smash them: if `x == y` both disappear, otherwise only a stone of weight `y − x` remains.

At the end at most one stone is left. Return the smallest possible weight of that stone, or `0` if none remains.
hints: However you smash, the final weight is a sum of the stones with + and − signs: some group minus the other group.
So the question is: split the stones into two groups with sums as close as possible.
Use a 0/1 knapsack to find the largest achievable sum S ≤ total / 2. The answer is total − 2S.
explain: The total weight is 23. Smashing stones is the same as splitting them into two groups and subtracting; the most even split is 11 against 12 (for example `[2,1,8]` against `[7,4,1]`). So the smallest possible final weight is 1.

title: Coin Change
summary: With unlimited coins of each denomination, return the fewest coins that make up amount, or -1 if impossible.
statement:
`coins` lists coin denominations, and you have an unlimited number of coins of each. Return the fewest coins needed to make exactly `amount`, or `-1` if it cannot be made.

Making an amount of 0 needs 0 coins.
hints: Always taking the largest coin first fails, for example with coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6.
Let best[a] be the fewest coins for amount a. best[a] = 1 + min(best[a − c]) over coins c ≤ a, with best[0] = 0.
Fill the table from 1 to amount, using a value larger than amount to mean "impossible". Watch out for coins larger than amount.
explain: 11 = 5 + 5 + 1 uses 3 coins, and no combination of 1, 2 and 5 makes 11 with fewer. So the answer is 3.

title: Coin Change II
summary: With unlimited coins of each denomination, return how many combinations (order doesn't matter) make up amount.
statement:
`coins` lists distinct coin denominations, with an unlimited supply of each. Return the number of different combinations of coins that add up to `amount`.

Order does not matter: `1 + 2` and `2 + 1` are the same combination. If no combination works, return `0`. The answer fits in a 32-bit integer.
hints: To count combinations rather than sequences, decide how many of each coin to use, one coin type at a time.
ways[a] counts combinations for amount a using the coins processed so far; ways[0] = 1.
Put the loop over coins outside and the loop over amounts (going up) inside: ways[a] += ways[a − coin]. Swapping the loops would count orderings instead.
explain: There are 4 ways to make 5: `5`, `2 + 2 + 1`, `2 + 1 + 1 + 1` and `1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1`. Order doesn't matter, so `1 + 2 + 2` is the same way as `2 + 2 + 1`.

title: Combination Sum IV
summary: Count the ordered sequences of values from nums (reuse allowed) that sum to target. Different orders count separately.
statement:
`nums` has distinct positive integers. Count the ordered sequences of values from `nums` (each value may be used any number of times) that add up to `target`.

Different orders count as different sequences, so `(1, 2)` and `(2, 1)` are both counted. The answer fits in a 32-bit integer.
hints: The last number of a sequence summing to t can be any value v ≤ t from nums.
So ways[t] = sum of ways[t − v] over all v ≤ t, with ways[0] = 1.
Here the loop over amounts is the outer loop, which is what makes order matter (the opposite of Coin Change II). Intermediate counts can overflow an int, so you may need to guard them.
explain: Here order matters. The sequences summing to 4 are (1,1,1,1), (1,1,2), (1,2,1), (2,1,1), (2,2), (1,3) and (3,1), so the answer is 7.

title: Perfect Squares
summary: Return the fewest perfect squares (1, 4, 9, …) that sum to n.
statement:
A perfect square is the square of an integer: 1, 4, 9, 16, … . Return the smallest number of perfect squares that add up to `n`.

The same square may be used more than once. Every number can be written as a sum of 1s, so an answer always exists.
hints: This is Coin Change where the coins are the squares up to n.
best[i] = 1 + min(best[i − k²]) over k with k² ≤ i, and best[0] = 0.
BFS over remainders also works. There is even a number-theory answer: it is always at most 4 (Lagrange's four-square theorem).
explain: 12 = 4 + 4 + 4 uses 3 perfect squares. It can't be done with 2 (no two squares add to 12) or with 1 (12 is not a square), so the answer is 3.

title: Ones and Zeroes
summary: Pick the largest subset of binary strings that uses at most m zeros and n ones in total. Return its size.

perf.label: 600 strings, m = n = 100
perf.gen: String[] a0 = BCB.words(600, 1, 10, "01"); int a1 = 100; int a2 = 100;

statement:
`strs` is a list of binary strings. Choose the largest possible subset of them such that, in total, the chosen strings contain at most `m` zeros and at most `n` ones.

Return the size of that subset.

Each string can be chosen at most once. The limits apply to the chosen strings together, counting every `0` and `1` character they contain.
hints: Each string is an item with two "weights" (its zeros and its ones) and a value of 1. It is a two-dimensional knapsack.
best[z][o] = the most strings you can pick with at most z zeros and o ones.
For each string with (zeros, ones), update best[z][o] = max(best[z][o], 1 + best[z − zeros][o − ones]), looping z and o downward so each string is used once.
explain: Choosing "10", "0001", "1" and "0" uses 1 + 3 + 0 + 1 = 5 zeros and 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 3 ones, exactly the limits. No 5 strings fit, so the answer is 4.
